lead: A WDM network carries many lightpaths, each on a wavelength. The nodes must add, drop and cross-connect those wavelengths without turning every signal into electronics. An optical add-drop multiplexer handles a few local wavelengths; an optical cross-connect switches many wavelengths between fiber pairs. A lightpath normally keeps one wavelength from end to end, called the wavelength continuity constraint, and converters are used only when that fails. Routing and wavelength assignment choose the path and the wavelength. These ideas run metro rings, data-centre links and long-haul mesh networks.
prereq: You need: the wavelength grid and components from 6.1 and 6.2, the lightpath idea from 6.5, and amplifier basics from 6.3.

sections.h3: Nodes that add, drop and cross-connect

blocks.text: An optical node does more than join fibers. It must add local wavelengths, drop wavelengths for local receivers, and pass the rest through. An optical add-drop multiplexer (OADM) does this for a few wavelengths. A fixed OADM drops one or two wavelengths using filters or gratings and circulators (see 6.2). A reconfigurable OADM uses a wavelength-selective switch (WSS), which sends each wavelength from an input to any chosen output. The WSS changes the path, not the wavelength.

An optical cross-connect (OXC) switches many wavelengths between many fiber pairs, so it can rearrange lightpaths. A metro ring uses OADMs to drop one wavelength for an apartment ISP while other wavelengths pass untouched. A long-haul mesh node uses an OXC.

Two OXC architectures are common. In broadcast-and-select, each input fiber is split into N copies, one copy for each output port. From each copy a filter picks the wanted wavelength, and a gate after the filter passes that wavelength or blocks it. A combiner then sums the one wavelength arriving from each input fiber to build that output port. Loss is splitter loss plus filter and gate loss plus combiner loss. A blocked gate still leaks a little, so the extinction ratio sets the crosstalk. In a WSS fabric, each input WSS routes each wavelength to a chosen output, and output combiners merge them. It filters instead of splitting all power to all outputs, so loss and crosstalk are lower, but cost is higher.

MEMS uses tiny tilting mirrors; LCoS uses liquid-crystal pixels; thermo-optic switches heat a waveguide to change its refractive index; electro-optic switches apply a voltage. MEMS and LCoS give low loss but millisecond switching. Electro-optic and SOA gates switch in nanoseconds, but the SOA gate adds noise and needs current.

A lightpath keeps one wavelength from source to destination unless a converter changes it. This is the wavelength continuity constraint. For a path with links 1 to k, let S_i be the set of free wavelengths on link i.

blocks.where: S_i is the set of free wavelengths on link i; k is the number of links; S is the set of wavelengths free on every link. The path works without conversion only if S is not empty.

blocks.text: Checking only pairs of links is wrong. Converters relax the rule. Optoelectronic regeneration receives the signal, reshapes and retimes it, and retransmits on a new wavelength; it may be electrical (see 6.3). Cross-gain modulation in a semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA) uses a strong pump at λ1 to modulate the gain seen by a probe at λ2. Four-wave mixing uses two pumps in a nonlinear medium to create an idler at a new wavelength. Converters are placed sparsely because each adds cost, loss and noise.

Routing and wavelength assignment (RWA) picks a path and a wavelength for each lightpath. In route-first-then-assign, find a route with Dijkstra, list the free wavelengths common to all its links, and take the first fit in a fixed order. If none is free, try the next route or block the request. Static traffic is known in advance and can be planned; dynamic traffic arrives and leaves, so blocking probability matters. RWA is graph colouring: each lightpath is a vertex, two vertices are joined if their paths share a fiber link, and colours are wavelengths. First-fit is a simple colouring heuristic.

Protection from 6.6 is reused: ring UPSR/BLSR and mesh 1+1 or shared backup. An OXC makes restoration fast by switching wavelengths. Optical burst switching (OBS) sends a control packet ahead on a separate wavelength, then a data burst after an offset time. Nodes configure before the burst arrives; contention can drop a burst. Optical packet switching (OPS) switches each packet, so it needs nanosecond switching, fast header processing and synchronization.

figure.caption: Links A–B, B–C and C–D offer different free wavelengths; no one wavelength is free on all three, so the lightpath A–B–C–D needs the converter at B.

spec.aria: A four-node line graph A to B to C to D; edges are labelled with free wavelengths, and node B is marked as having a wavelength converter.

examples.question: A lightpath must run A-B-C-D. Link A-B has λ1 and λ2 free, B-C has λ2 and λ3 free, C-D has λ1 and λ3 free. (a) Can it be set up with wavelength continuity? (b) What happens if node B has a converter? (c) How many switch elements does a full optical cross-connect need with 4 fiber pairs and 8 wavelengths per pair?
steps: Write the free sets: S_AB = {λ1, λ2}, S_BC = {λ2, λ3}, S_CD = {λ1, λ3}.

For continuity, intersect all three: {λ1, λ2} ∩ {λ2, λ3} = {λ2}; then {λ2} ∩ {λ1, λ3} = ∅. The intersection is empty, so no single wavelength is free on all three links. The path is blocked without conversion.

With one converter at B: use λ2 on A-B, because λ2 is free on A-B. At B, convert λ2 to λ3. λ3 is free on B-C and also free on C-D, so the rest of the path runs on λ3 without a second conversion. One converter at B is enough.
Full OXC: incoming wavelengths = 4 fiber pairs × 8 wavelengths per pair = 32. Outgoing ports = 32. A full cross-connect needs one switch element for each input-output pair: 32 × 32 = 1024 elements.
examples.answer: The path is blocked without conversion (0 common wavelengths). A single converter at B (λ2 on A-B, converted to λ3 for B-C and C-D) makes it work. A full 4×8 OXC needs 1024 switch elements.

traps: A common wavelength on each pair of links is not enough. The same wavelength must be free on every link of the path.
A WSS switches a wavelength; it does not change it. Only a wavelength converter changes λ1 to λ2.
For a full OXC, multiply fiber pairs by wavelengths per pair first, then square. 4×8 gives 32×32, not 4×8 elements.
Splitter loss in dB adds: a 1:16 splitter gives 10 log₁₀ 16 ≈ 12 dB, and an output combiner adds another 12 dB.
OADM and OXC are not the same: an OADM touches only local add/drop wavelengths, while an OXC can switch every wavelength between every port.

quiz.q: State the job of an OADM.
quiz.a: An OADM adds local wavelengths into a fiber, drops local wavelengths out, and passes the other wavelengths through unchanged.

quiz.q: Why is a WSS called wavelength-selective, and what does it not do?
quiz.a: It routes each wavelength separately from an input to a chosen output, so it selects by wavelength. It does not convert a wavelength to a different value.

quiz.q: Link A-B has λ1 and λ3 free; link B-C has λ2 and λ3 free. Can a lightpath A-B-C use one wavelength without a converter? Which one?
quiz.a: Intersect the sets: {λ1, λ3} ∩ {λ2, λ3} = {λ3}. Yes, use λ3 on both links.

quiz.q: A broadcast-and-select OXC splits each input 1:16 (16 arms), with one gate and one output combiner in the path. Estimate the splitter loss and explain why amplifiers may be needed.
quiz.a: A 1:16 splitter gives 10 log₁₀ 16 ≈ 12 dB loss. The output combiner adds about 12 dB more, plus gate loss, so total loss exceeds 24 dB; an EDFA or SOA is needed to recover the level.

quiz.q: A full OXC has 6 fiber pairs and 16 wavelengths per pair. How many switch elements does it need?
quiz.a: Incoming wavelengths = 6 × 16 = 96. A full cross-connect needs 96 × 96 = 9216 switch elements.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one cost of placing a wavelength converter at every node.
quiz.a: Advantage: the wavelength continuity constraint disappears, so blocking falls and wavelengths can be reused more freely. Cost: every converter adds cost, insertion loss, power consumption and noise, and needs management, so sparse placement is usually better.

quiz.q: In OBS, what is the offset time?
quiz.a: The time between sending the control packet and sending the data burst, so intermediate nodes can configure before the burst arrives.

quiz.q: Why does OPS need faster switching than OBS?
quiz.a: OPS switches every packet, and packets last nanoseconds to microseconds. OBS switches once per burst, and a burst lasts much longer, so OBS gives nodes more time to reconfigure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern metro and data-centre networks use reconfigurable ROADMs with WSS fabrics and flex-grid optics, where the wavelength grid itself can change. Software-defined networking puts RWA and restoration in a central controller. Research moves from OBS and OPS toward deterministic optical switching for AI clusters. Search for “elastic optical network”, “ROADM architecture” and “spectrum assignment”.
